name: Chapter 11: Organisms and Populations
description: Population attributes, density, growth models, life history, and interactions: predation, competition, parasitism, commensalism, mutualism

cards.term: Who is the Father of Ecology in India?
cards.definition: Ramdeo Misra (BHU, Varanasi)
How: mechanism of a process. Why: significance of the process.

cards.term: Example: bulbul singing: how and why?
cards.definition: How: voice box and vibrating bone. Why: to communicate with its mate in the breeding season.
Study of interactions among organisms and between organisms and their physical (abiotic) environment

cards.term: Four levels of organisation in ecology?
cards.definition: Organisms, populations, communities, biomes
Individuals of a species in a well-defined area sharing/competing for resources and potentially interbreeding
Yes, for ecological studies
Cormorants in a wetland, rats in a dwelling, teakwood trees in a forest, bacteria on a plate, lotus plants in a pond
Natural selection operates at the population level; links ecology to population genetics and evolution

cards.term: Attributes of a population but not an individual (Exercise 1)?
cards.definition: Birth rate, death rate, sex ratio, age distribution, population density
0.4 per lotus per year

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Birth rate

20 lotus plants; 8 new plants added in a year. Birth rate?

Per capita rate = new ÷ initial.
  1. Births = 8
  2. Initial population = 20
  3. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Birth rate

20 lotus plants; 8 new plants added in a year. Birth rate?

Per capita rate = new ÷ initial.
  1. Births = 8
  2. Initial population = 20
  3. Birth rate = 8/20 = 0.4 offspring per lotus per year

cards.definition: 0.1 per fruitfly per week

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Death rate

4 of 40 fruitflies die in a week. Death rate?

Per capita rate = deaths ÷ population.
  1. Deaths = 4
  2. Population = 40
  3. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Death rate

4 of 40 fruitflies die in a week. Death rate?

Per capita rate = deaths ÷ population.
  1. Deaths = 4
  2. Population = 40
  3. Death rate = 4/40 = 0.1 per fruitfly per week

cards.definition: Plot of age distribution (per cent individuals of each age group), for males and females
Expanding (broad base, growing), stable, declining (narrow base)

cards.term: Three age groups in a pyramid?
cards.definition: Pre-reproductive, reproductive, post-reproductive

cards.term: What does a broad pre-reproductive base indicate? (intuition)
cards.definition: Many young individuals about to reproduce → growing population

cards.term: Examples of small and huge population sizes?
cards.definition: < 10 Siberian cranes at Bharatpur; millions of Chlamydomonas in a pond
Population density (N)

cards.term: When is number not a good measure of density?
cards.definition: E.g. one huge banyan vs 200 Parthenium plants: use per cent cover or biomass

cards.term: Best measure of density for dense bacterial culture?
cards.definition: Biomass/turbidity rather than counting
Number of fish caught per trap
Indirectly using pug marks and fecal pellets

cards.text: Density increases by {{c1::natality}} and {{c2::immigration}}; decreases by {{c3::mortality}} and {{c4::emigration}}.

cards.definition: Natality: number of births in a period. Mortality: number of deaths in a period.
Immigration: individuals of the same species coming in. Emigration: individuals leaving.

cards.term: Equation for population density at t + 1?
Most important factors under normal conditions?
cards.definition: Births and deaths

cards.term: When is immigration more important than births?
cards.definition: When a new habitat is just being colonised
When resources (food, space) are unlimited
\( \frac{dN}{dt} = rN \), where \( r = b - d \)
Intrinsic rate of natural increase: per capita births minus deaths
Norway rat: 0.015; Flour beetle: 0.12; Human population, India (1981): 0.0205

Doubling each square (1, 2, 4, 8…) quickly exceeds a kingdom’s wheat: exponential growth explodes
r ≈ 0.231 per year

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Exercise 2

Population doubles in 3 years. Find r.

Use \( N_t = N_0 e^{rt} \).
  1. 2N₀ = N₀ e^{3r}
  2. ln 2 = 3r
  3. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 2

Population doubles in 3 years. Find r.

Use \( N_t = N_0 e^{rt} \).
  1. 2N₀ = N₀ e^{3r}
  2. ln 2 = 3r
  3. r = 0.693 / 3 = 0.231 per year

cards.definition: Maximum number a habitat’s resources can support
Lag → acceleration → deceleration → asymptote at K

cards.term: Name and shape of logistic growth?
cards.definition: Verhulst–Pearl logistic growth; sigmoid (S-shaped) curve
\( \frac{dN}{dt} = rN \left( \frac{K - N}{K} \right) \)

cards.term: What does (K − N)/K do in the logistic equation? (intuition)
cards.definition: It is the fraction of space left: near zero when N ≈ K, so growth slows to zero

cards.term: Which growth model is more realistic, and why?
cards.definition: Logistic: resources are finite and become limiting

cards.term: Read Figure 11.3: curve a vs b?
cards.definition: (a) Exponential (J), responses not limiting. (b) Logistic (S), responses limiting; flattens at K.

cards.term: What do populations evolve to maximise?
cards.definition: Reproductive (Darwinian) fitness (high r)
Pacific salmon fish, bamboo
Most birds and mammals

cards.term: Many small offspring vs few large offspring?
cards.definition: Many small: oysters, pelagic fishes. Few large: birds, mammals.
Constraints of the abiotic and biotic components of the habitat

cards.term: Can a habitat have just one species?
cards.definition: No; even a plant needs soil microbes and pollinators
Interactions between populations of two different species
+ / +: Mutualism; − / −: Competition; + / − (eats): Predation; + / − (lives on/in): Parasitism; + / 0: Commensalism; − / 0: Amensalism

cards.definition: CoMmensalism = one gets a "Meal/benefit" (+/0). Amensalism = one gets "Ache" (−/0).

cards.term: Which interactions involve species living closely together?
cards.definition: Predation, parasitism, commensalism
(d) One benefits, the other is affected (harmed)
Nature’s way of transferring energy fixed by plants to higher trophic levels

cards.term: Is a sparrow eating seeds a predator?
cards.definition: Yes; herbivores are broadly predators too
Energy conduits; keep prey populations under control; maintain species diversity by reducing competition among prey

cards.term: Why do exotic species become invasive?
cards.definition: The invaded land lacks their natural predators
Introduced in 1920s, spread over millions of hectares; controlled by a cactus-feeding moth from its native habitat
Ability of the predator to regulate prey population
Removing the starfish Pisaster from intertidal areas made 10+ invertebrate species extinct within a year due to competition
Over-exploiting prey would make the prey and then the predator extinct
Camouflage (cryptic colouring in insects, frogs), being poisonous

cards.term: Why is the Monarch butterfly distasteful to birds?
cards.definition: A special chemical acquired by its caterpillar from feeding on a poisonous weed

cards.term: What fraction of insects are phytophagous?
cards.definition: Nearly 25%

cards.term: Why is herbivory severe for plants?
cards.definition: Plants cannot run away
Thorns (Acacia, cactus); chemicals that sicken, deter, disrupt reproduction or kill
It produces highly poisonous cardiac glycosides

cards.term: Commercial plant chemicals that are actually defences?
cards.definition: Nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine, opium
Cryptic colouring to avoid detection; e.g. insects and frogs blending with background

cards.term: Does competition occur only among related species?
cards.definition: No; e.g. flamingoes and fishes compete for zooplankton in South American lakes
Not always; interference competition reduces feeding efficiency even when resources are abundant
Fitness (r) of one species is significantly lower in the presence of another
Became extinct within a decade after goats were introduced on Galapagos (better browsing efficiency)
A species restricted by a superior competitor expands its range when the competitor is removed
On Scottish rocky coasts, larger Balanus excludes smaller Chthamalus from the intertidal zone
Chthamalus

cards.term: Who are more affected by competition?
cards.definition: Herbivores and plants more than carnivores
Two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot co-exist indefinitely; the inferior one is eliminated
Competing species avoid competition by different feeding times or foraging patterns
Five closely related warbler species on the same tree co-existed through behavioural differences in foraging
Flamingoes and resident fishes competing for zooplankton

cards.term: Why has parasitism evolved so widely?
cards.definition: It ensures free lodging and meals
Host evolves resistance, parasite evolves counter-mechanisms (host-specific parasites)
Loss of unnecessary sense organs, adhesive organs/suckers, loss of digestive system, high reproductive capacity

cards.term: Hosts of the human liver fluke?
cards.definition: Two intermediate hosts: a snail and a fish
Reduce survival, growth, reproduction, population density; make hosts vulnerable to predation
Parasites maximise their own reproduction; using host resources inevitably causes some harm
Lice on humans, ticks on dogs, copepods on marine fish, Cuscuta on hedge plants
Lost chlorophyll and leaves; takes nutrition from host plant

cards.term: Why is the female mosquito not a parasite?
cards.definition: It only takes a blood meal briefly for reproduction; does not live on the host
Live inside the host (liver, kidney, lungs, RBCs); complex life cycles, simplified bodies, high reproductive potential
Parasitic bird lays eggs in the host’s nest for incubation; cuckoo (koel) in crow’s nest
Eggs resemble host eggs in size and colour
Orchid epiphyte on mango; barnacles on whale; cattle egret and cattle; clown fish and sea anemone
Commensalism: orchid benefits, mango unaffected

cards.term: Why does the egret follow cattle?
cards.definition: Moving cattle flush out insects for the egret
Fish gets protection among stinging tentacles; anemone gains nothing apparent
Lichens (fungus + alga/cyanobacteria), mycorrhizae (fungus + roots), plant–pollinator relations
Fungi help nutrient absorption; plant gives carbohydrates
Pollen and nectar for pollinators; juicy fruits for seed dispersers

cards.term: Why do plant–animal interactions involve co-evolution?
cards.definition: To safeguard against cheaters (nectar thieves); flower and pollinator evolution are tightly linked
One-to-one: each fig species pollinated only by its partner wasp; wasp lays eggs in fruit and larvae eat some developing seeds
Sexual deceit: a petal resembles the female bee; the male "pseudocopulates" and transfers pollen

cards.term: Why must Ophrys co-evolve with the bee?
cards.definition: If the female bee’s pattern changes, pollination success drops unless the petal keeps resembling her
Population: individuals of one species in an area. Community: populations of different species interacting in an area.

Fig and wasp: Mutualism; Cuckoo and crow: Brood parasitism; Balanus and Chthamalus: Competition; Cattle egret and cattle: Commensalism; Prickly pear and moth: Predation (biocontrol); Cuscuta and hedge plant: Parasitism
